The Extreme Value Theorem. It asserts that a continuous function on a closed and bounded interval from a to b attains both a maximum and a minimum value. This seemingly obvious fact is profound. It connects the algebraic property of continuity to the geometric existence of extreme points. Yet it is false in weaker settings, such as on open intervals or for discontinuous functions. The Extreme Value Theorem is a cornerstone of calculus, enabling existence proofs and optimization algorithms.

The statement is straightforward: if f is continuous on the closed interval from a to b, then f achieves a maximum value M and a minimum value m on that interval. However, the theorem requires both continuity and closure. The function must have no jumps or discontinuities, and the interval must include its endpoints, written as the closed interval from a to b, not just open endpoints. The Extreme Value Theorem fails if either condition is absent.

On an open interval from a to b, a continuous function may not achieve its supremum or infimum. For example, the function f of x equals x on the open interval from zero to one approaches but never reaches one, and approaches but never reaches zero. The proof of the Extreme Value Theorem relies on the Heine-Borel theorem: closed and bounded sets in the real numbers are compact, and continuous images of compact sets are compact. This compactness preserves the existence of extrema.

The Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that optimization problems have solutions. There is no need to worry that a function merely approaches a bound without reaching it. The maximum and minimum actually occur at some points. The proof essentially combines compactness with continuity. Closed and bounded sets in the reals are compact, and functions preserve the topological property of compactness, ensuring image sets are compact and thus bounded and closed.

The theorem is used in the proof of the Intermediate Value Theorem and in analysis of critical points for calculus. Both depend on the existence properties that the Extreme Value Theorem establishes. It generalizes to compact sets in any metric space or topological space: continuous functions on compact spaces are bounded and attain their extrema. This makes the Extreme Value Theorem a cornerstone of topology and analysis. Applications span optimization in calculus and economics, numerical analysis for finding global minima, and physics through the principle of least energy.
